title: Schools banning cell phones? A parent’s survival guide
summary: Learn why schools ban cell phones, how to stay connected in emergencies, and ways to help your child adjust.
body_markdown:
Schools across the country are implementing cell phone bans in an effort to improve learning in our digitally addicted age—and alleviate constant distraction for children. This primer can help you and your child create a better experience, both in and out of the classroom.


## Why are schools banning cell phones?


In pre-digital times, when a teacher said, "Pay attention!" it was typically because Susie and Debbie were passing notes, or the boys in the back of the room were horsing around.


Today, the distraction is smartphones. Saying, "No phones in class!" is about as effective as "Pay attention!" used to be: that is, not very effective.


Educators have been grappling with digital technologies in schools for at least 40 years, beginning when students started bringing pagers to school in the 1980s. In a 2025 survey, The National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) School Pulse Panel revealed that more than half of public school leaders say[cell phones hurt academic performance](https://ies.ed.gov/learn/press-release/more-half-public-school-leaders-say-cell-phones-hurt-academic-performance) .


## Is my child's state banning cell phones?


States began passing cell phone policies in 2023, starting with Florida. This inaugural phone ban took place after social psychologists posited that phones were having a negative effect—not just on academic performance, but on students' mental health.


While the statewide ban covered instructional time only, one district imposed[a stricter policy](https://www.nber.org/digest/202512/school-cell-phone-bans-and-student-achievement?page=1&perPage=50) requiring cell phones to be silenced and stored all day. The result? Significantly better test scores, especially for male students in middle and high school.


These outcomes generated action among educators nationwide. As of August 2026,[45 states had enacted laws or policies](https://ballotpedia.org/State_policies_on_cellphone_use_in_K-12_public_schools) regulating classroom cell phone usage for grades K-12.


Five states have[not issued a statewide ban](https://ballotpedia.org/State_policies_on_cellphone_use_in_K-12_public_schools) on cell phones in schools: Wyoming, South Dakota, Mississippi, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts, leaving smartphone use during school hours up to local districts.


If your state is one of the 45 that have enacted a statewide phone ban, you can review the specific details on the policy and type of limitation[here](https://ballotpedia.org/State_policies_on_cellphone_use_in_K-12_public_schools) .


## Do school phone bans actually work?


Restricting mobile phones in school has[led to more focused classrooms](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/angela-duckworth-over-20000-educators-share-insights-school-cell-phone-policies) , according to survey results from 20,000 public school teachers nationwide.


The stricter the policy, the better the outcome: requiring students to leave phones in hallway lockers or a locked phone pouch yields stronger compliance than allowing students to carry their phones in backpacks or back pockets.


Angela Duckworth, a professor of psychology at the University of Pennsylvania who led the research initiative, explains[why stricter policies work better:](https://www.edweek.org/technology/do-school-cellphone-bans-work-what-early-findings-tell-us/2025/10) "In psychology, there is a principle that could be summarized as physical distance creates psychological distance. When you are in the presence of a temptation, the closer it is to you, the more tempting it is."


[Kids themselves approve of phone bans](https://www.edweek.org/technology/how-cellphone-bans-have-affected-students-lives-what-teens-say/2026/01) . According to new research from Education Week, 67% of teens said their school's cell phone restrictions "have had no impact" on making friends. However, they also reported that banning cell phones hasn't affected their ability to pay attention or altered their stress levels. The lack of perceived negative effects could be due to the survey being done at the start of the school year, when the cell phone ban was new.


Their optimism might also be due to the truth that a school smartphone ban simply shifts the timeline: kids may stay up later and move their social media activity to nighttime.


"School phone policies alone are not enough to tackle some of the issues that we're seeing in adolescents," says University of Birmingham Professor Vicky Goodyear in conversation with Harvard sociologist Carrie James.


In a[study of more than 1200 students](https://www.gse.harvard.edu/ideas/edcast/25/09/banning-cellphones-quick-fix-or-false-hope) , Goodyear found "no differences in mental health, academic performance, or well-being between schools with strict bans and those without. While restrictions cut down on in-school phone use, they didn't meaningfully reduce students' overall daily screen time."


## What do teachers and parents think?


According to The Pew Research Center, 72% of U.S. high school teachers say[cell phone distraction is a major problem in class](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/06/12/72-percent-of-us-high-school-teachers-say-cellphone-distraction-is-a-major-problem-in-the-classroom/) . And while more Americans now support rather than oppose school cell phone bans during the school day, enacting a policy is only the first step.


Enforcing a cell phone ban in schools is the challenging part, especially in high school. Younger children are more compliant with adult authority; by high school, six in ten teachers say phone bans are much more difficult to enforce. This is partly due to[pervasive cell phone availability among teens](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/12/11/teens-social-media-and-technology-2023/) : a 2023 Pew survey indicated 95% of U.S. teenagers ages 13 to 17 have access to a smartphone.


Parents agree: while 77% of adults support in-class cell phone bans for middle- and high school students, nearly half say[all-day phone bans](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/07/29/more-americans-now-support-than-oppose-all-day-school-cellphone-bans/) make the most sense.


This corresponds with Duckworth's psychological insight: keeping those distractions away all day makes for a more focused, productive learning environment.


## How will I reach my child in an emergency?


Parental concern about reaching their child with schools banning cell phones is a recent phenomenon. For decades, if a parent needed to get in touch with their child during the day, they called the school's front office.


In an emergency affecting everyone, typically the school administrator would broadcast a message via the public address system.


However, in the modern era, "Most parents gave their kids cell phones so they could have[immediate access to communicate](https://hub.jhu.edu/2024/09/23/school-cell-phone-bans-qa/) ," explains Annette C. Anderson, deputy director of Johns Hopkins Center for Safe and Healthy Schools and assistant professor in the Johns Hopkins School of Education.


With phone bans, an Apple Watch is a great potential first step for keeping in contact with your child, because parents can track student location via Apple's Find My service. Even if your child's school bans Apple Watches as well as smartphones during the school day, parents can use the Watch to track their kids before and after school. And, of course, they can be used to receive texts and make phone calls if needed in an emergency.


If your school forbids Apple Watches during the school day, contacting the administrative office remains the most reliable way to reach your child quickly. Make sure the school office, school nurse, and other relevant numbers are saved to your Contacts.


If the school permits it, you might also consider investing in a basic flip phone as an alternative device for school hours, with the caveat that it is only to be used to call home in an emergency.


## How can I help my child adjust to a phone ban?


- [Calm your own anxiety](https://momentousinstitute.org/resources/worried-about-the-cell-phone-ban-in-schools-here-are-3-ways-parents-can-cope-with-anxiety/) , advises the Momentous Institute, a mental health organization dedicated to creating healthier families and communities. The more you practice self-care, the more you will model resilience for your child in new or difficult circumstances, such as phone bans.
- Validate your child's stress. Assure them they may feel less anxiety without constant notifications, especially since the ban affects all students so they won’t feel left out socially. Focus on the positives, such as more face-to-face communication and better attention in class. You can also create some[healthy tech habits for kids](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/school-year-guide-healthy-tech-habits-for-kids/) at home, like no screens before school. This way, they're entering the learning environment primed to study, not scroll.
- Check whether your child's school has a[phone ban emergency contact plan](https://nappot.com/school-phone-ban-tween-emergency-contact-plan/) in place. Such a plan will outline the approved steps the school can use to reach you in the event of an emergency.
- Encourage low-tech means of self-expression, such as journaling or reading. Gift your child a beautiful journal and rollerball pen to get them started. Helpful, specific[back-to-school communication](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/back-to-school-communication-habits-reduce-stress/) habits can reduce stress—it just requires clarity and focus, which start with the parents.
- Consider getting a[MyPhone home phone](https://www.ooma.com/home-phone-service/myphone/) : a landline for kids that's screen-free, fun, and safe. You can schedule "quiet hours" for homework or playtime and monitor all incoming and outgoing calls via the call log. Kids will love the party line, which enables three-way calling, and the built-in answering machine, which preserves precious voicemails, like those from Grandma. Bonus: Using a MyPhone landline will also minimize smartphone use at home!


## Questions to ask your school


Some suggested questions to ask your child's school about phone bans:


### Emergency and safety questions


- How will I reach my child in an emergency?
- How do students contact parents in a crisis? Are landlines available?
- What happens to phones during a lockdown? Can students access their phones in a shelter-in-place or other emergency?
- Do you make medical exceptions?


### Storage and liability


- Where are phones kept during the day?
- Who is responsible for lost or damaged devices? If a phone is stored in a school-provided pouch, bin, or locker, does the school cover damage or theft?
- Does the phone ban cover passing periods and lunch?
- What counts as a "phone"? Do the rules include a smartwatch, tablet, or basic flip phones?


### Enforcement


- What happens if a child breaks the rules?
- Who has the authority to confiscate a device? Can any staff member take a phone?
- Are there exceptions for class projects? Can teachers temporarily allow devices for digital learning or research?


While a cell phone ban in schools is just one piece of the puzzle in the digital age, it's a useful start for a more productive learning environment, and may even result in happier, calmer kids.
